title: Build a second implementation on a new branch instead of extending PR #5
context: A stdlib-only Python shortener already exists on the url-shortener branch with draft PR #5. Asked how to proceed, the user chose to start fresh on a new branch.
options: Continue url-shortener: no rework, but keeps that design
Start fresh from main on a new branch: leaves PR #5 untouched, two implementations exist until one is dropped
Rebuild on top of url-shortener: PR #5 would show the new code, history gets muddled
choice: Start fresh from main on branch shorty-fastapi
why: The user picked this option when asked. The package is named shorty rather than shortener so the two branches do not collide if both are ever merged.

title: FastAPI rather than the standard library or Flask
context: The user asked only for a URL shortener in Python. The repo had no dependencies or tooling.
options: Standard library http.server: nothing to install, but routing, JSON parsing, body limits and error responses are hand-written
Flask: small and familiar, request validation and API docs still by hand
FastAPI + uvicorn: typed request and response models, validation and an interactive /docs page for free, at the cost of an install step
why: It removes the hand-rolled HTTP plumbing, and /docs doubles as the UI so no HTML form is needed. The cost is that the service now needs pip install before it runs.

title: Random 7-character base62 codes with retry on collision
context: Each link needs a short code that is unique and safe to put in a URL.
options: Base62 of an auto-increment id: shortest possible, no collisions, but codes are guessable and reveal how many links exist
Hash of the URL: deterministic, but forces deduplication and still needs collision handling
Random base62 from secrets, retry on primary-key conflict: not enumerable, about 3.5 trillion codes, tiny collision chance
choice: Random base62 from secrets, 7 characters, up to 10 attempts
why: Sequential codes let anyone walk every link in the service. Uniqueness is enforced by the primary key, so a collision is caught by the database rather than by a check-then-insert race.

title: Shortening the same URL twice creates two separate links
context: A caller may submit a URL that is already stored.
options: Return the existing code: fewer rows, but every caller shares one click count and the URL column needs an index
Always create a new link: more rows, each link has its own count and nobody learns whether a URL was already shortened
why: Per-link click counts stay meaningful to whoever created the link, and it avoids revealing that someone else already shortened a URL.

title: One SQLite connection per operation, WAL mode
context: FastAPI runs these sync handlers on a thread pool, and sqlite3 connections are not meant to be shared across threads.
options: One shared connection behind a lock: fastest per call, serialises all reads
Connection per operation: a little slower per call, no shared state, safe across threads and processes
SQLAlchemy or a connection pool: more machinery than four queries need
choice: Connection per operation with WAL and a 5 second busy timeout
why: It is correct under threads and multiple uvicorn workers without any locking code. Opening a local SQLite file is cheap enough at this scale.

title: Redirect with 302 and count clicks in the same statement
context: Following a short link must redirect and increment the click counter.
options: 301 permanent: browsers cache it, so repeat visits skip the server and clicks are undercounted
302 temporary: every visit reaches the server and is counted
SELECT then UPDATE: two statements, two round trips
UPDATE ... RETURNING url: one atomic statement, needs SQLite 3.35+
why: Click counts are only accurate if the redirect is not cached. A single statement makes lookup and increment atomic; SQLite 3.35 shipped in 2021 and is bundled with every supported Python on Windows and macOS.

anchors.snippet: "UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 WHERE code = ? RETURNING url",

title: Own URL validator that stores the URL as given, http and https only
context: The service redirects visitors to whatever it stored, so it must refuse javascript:, data: and header-injection payloads.
options: pydantic HttpUrl: no code to write, but it rewrites the URL (adds a trailing slash, punycodes hosts) and reports failures as 422
Own check on urlsplit: a few lines to maintain, URL stored byte-for-byte, clear 400 messages
choice: Own check: http/https scheme, a host, no whitespace or control characters, at most 2048 characters
why: A shortener should redirect to exactly what the user pasted. It does not block private or internal hosts, because the server never fetches the URL itself.

title: No HTML form, expiry, deletion or authentication in this first version
context: The request was a URL shortener with no further requirements.
options: Add a web form, link expiry, delete endpoint and API keys now: more to review, guessed requirements
Ship shorten, redirect, custom alias and click stats; / redirects to the generated /docs page
choice: Ship the core and point / at /docs
why: Those features depend on how the service will be used, which has not been said. Anyone who can reach the server can create links, so it binds to 127.0.0.1 by default.
